items.readable_text:
Content:
When dealing with sums of square roots, we can combine any terms with the same number under the square root symbol [MATH: \sqrt{\phantom 0}.]

Content:
For example, consider the following expression:

Content:
[MATH: 2\sqrt 5 + 4\sqrt 5]

Content:
Remember that [MATH: 2\sqrt 5] and [MATH: 4\sqrt 5] mean [MATH: 2\cdot\sqrt 5] and [MATH: 4\cdot\sqrt 5,] respectively.

Content:
We can simplify our expression by combining the two radicals, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: 2sqrt(5) + 4sqrt(5)|=; (2 + 4)sqrt(5)|=; 6sqrt(5)]

Content:
Similarly,

Content:
[MATH: 2sqrt(7) − sqrt(7)|=; 2sqrt(7) − 1 ⋅ sqrt(7)|=; (2 − 1)sqrt(7)|=; 1 ⋅ sqrt(7)|=; sqrt(7).]

Content:
However, we cannot combine terms when the numbers under the radical are different. For example, the expression

Content:
[MATH: 2\sqrt 3 + \sqrt 5]

Content:
cannot be simplified because there is no way of combining [MATH: \sqrt 3] and [MATH: \sqrt 5.]

Content:
Recall that the product rule for radicals states that

Content:
[MATH: \sqrt{a\cdot b} = \sqrt{a}\cdot \sqrt{b}]

Content:
where [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are nonnegative numbers.

Content:
We can use the product rule for radicals to simplify some expressions. Let's see an example.

items.title: Simplifying Square Root Expressions Using the Product Rule for Radicals

sections.readable_text: Simplify the expression [MATH: 3\sqrt{80} -8\sqrt{5}.]
EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we use the product rule for radicals to simplify [MATH: \sqrt{80},] as follows:

[MATH: sqrt(80)|= sqrt(16 ⋅ 5) = sqrt(16) ⋅ sqrt(5) = 4sqrt(5)]

As a result,

[MATH: 3sqrt(80) − 8sqrt(5)|=; 3(4sqrt(5)) − 8sqrt(5)|=; 12sqrt(5) − 8sqrt(5).]

Now, we can combine the two [MATH: \sqrt{5}] terms together:

[MATH: 12sqrt(5) − 8sqrt(5)|=; (12 − 8)sqrt(5)|=; 4sqrt(5)]

items.readable_text:
Content:
We can simplify cube root expressions in the same way as with square roots.

Content:
For example, consider the following expression:

Content:
[MATH: 4\sqrt[3]2 - 6\sqrt[3] 2]

Content:
We can simplify our expression by combining the two radicals, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: 4root(2, 3) − 6root(2, 3)|=; (4 − 6)root(2, 3)|=; − 2root(2, 3)]

Content:
As with square roots, we cannot combine terms when the numbers under the radical are different. For example, the expression

Content:
[MATH: 3\sqrt[3] 2 + \sqrt[3] 5]

Content:
cannot be simplified because there is no way of combining [MATH: \sqrt[3] 2] and [MATH: \sqrt[3] 5.]

Content:
Finally, it is not possible to combine square root and cube root terms -- not even if the numbers under the radical symbol are the same! For example, the expression

Content:
[MATH: 4\sqrt 2 + \sqrt[3] 2]

Content:
cannot be simplified because there is no way of combining [MATH: \sqrt 2] and [MATH: \sqrt[3] 2.]

First, we use the product rule for radicals, as follows:

[MATH: root(40, 3)|= root(8 ⋅ 5, 3) = root(8, 3) ⋅ root(5, 3) = 2root(5, 3)]

As a result, we have

[MATH: 2root(5, 3) + 5sqrt(10) − 3root(40, 3)|=; 2root(5, 3) + 5sqrt(10) − 3(2root(5, 3))|=; 2root(5, 3) + 5sqrt(10) − 6root(5, 3).]

Now, we can combine the two [MATH: \sqrt[3]{5}] terms together:

[MATH: 2root(5, 3) + 5sqrt(10) − 6root(5, 3)|=; 5sqrt(10) + (2root(5, 3) − 6root(5, 3))|=; 5sqrt(10) + (2 − 6)root(5, 3)|=; 5sqrt(10) − 4root(5, 3)]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
When dealing with sums of square roots, we can combine any terms with the same number under the square root symbol [MATH: \sqrt{\phantom 0}.]

Content:
For example, consider the following expression:

Content:
[MATH: 2\sqrt 5 + 4\sqrt 5]

Content:
Remember that [MATH: 2\sqrt 5] and [MATH: 4\sqrt 5] mean [MATH: 2\cdot\sqrt 5] and [MATH: 4\cdot\sqrt 5,] respectively.

Content:
We can simplify our expression by combining the two radicals, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: 2sqrt(5) + 4sqrt(5)|=; (2 + 4)sqrt(5)|=; 6sqrt(5)]

Content:
Similarly,

Content:
[MATH: 2sqrt(7) − sqrt(7)|=; 2sqrt(7) − 1 ⋅ sqrt(7)|=; (2 − 1)sqrt(7)|=; 1 ⋅ sqrt(7)|=; sqrt(7).]

Content:
However, we cannot combine terms when the numbers under the radical are different. For example, the expression

Content:
[MATH: 2\sqrt 3 + \sqrt 5]

Content:
cannot be simplified because there is no way of combining [MATH: \sqrt 3] and [MATH: \sqrt 5.]

[MATH: 8sqrt(3) − 5sqrt(3) + sqrt(5)|=; (8 − 5)sqrt(3) + sqrt(5)|=; 3sqrt(3) + sqrt(5)]

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Product Rule for Radicals

Content:
Recall that the product rule for radicals states that

Content:
[MATH: \sqrt{a\cdot b} = \sqrt{a}\cdot \sqrt{b}]

Content:
where [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are nonnegative numbers.

Content:
We can use the product rule for radicals to simplify some expressions. Let's see an example.

Item 6 — Example: Simplifying Square Root Expressions Using the Product Rule for Radicals

Example Prompt:
Simplify the expression [MATH: 3\sqrt{80} -8\sqrt{5}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we use the product rule for radicals to simplify [MATH: \sqrt{80},] as follows:

[MATH: sqrt(80)|= sqrt(16 ⋅ 5) = sqrt(16) ⋅ sqrt(5) = 4sqrt(5)]

As a result,

[MATH: 3sqrt(80) − 8sqrt(5)|=; 3(4sqrt(5)) − 8sqrt(5)|=; 12sqrt(5) − 8sqrt(5).]

Now, we can combine the two [MATH: \sqrt{5}] terms together:

[MATH: 12sqrt(5) − 8sqrt(5)|=; (12 − 8)sqrt(5)|=; 4sqrt(5)]

Item 9 — Tutorial: Simplifying Expressions With Cube Roots

Content:
We can simplify cube root expressions in the same way as with square roots.

Content:
For example, consider the following expression:

Content:
[MATH: 4\sqrt[3]2 - 6\sqrt[3] 2]

Content:
We can simplify our expression by combining the two radicals, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: 4root(2, 3) − 6root(2, 3)|=; (4 − 6)root(2, 3)|=; − 2root(2, 3)]

Content:
As with square roots, we cannot combine terms when the numbers under the radical are different. For example, the expression

Content:
[MATH: 3\sqrt[3] 2 + \sqrt[3] 5]

Content:
cannot be simplified because there is no way of combining [MATH: \sqrt[3] 2] and [MATH: \sqrt[3] 5.]

Content:
Finally, it is not possible to combine square root and cube root terms -- not even if the numbers under the radical symbol are the same! For example, the expression

Content:
[MATH: 4\sqrt 2 + \sqrt[3] 2]

Content:
cannot be simplified because there is no way of combining [MATH: \sqrt 2] and [MATH: \sqrt[3] 2.]

EXPLANATION

[MATH: root(40, 3)|= root(8 ⋅ 5, 3) = root(8, 3) ⋅ root(5, 3) = 2root(5, 3)]

[MATH: 2root(5, 3) + 5sqrt(10) − 3root(40, 3)|=; 2root(5, 3) + 5sqrt(10) − 3(2root(5, 3))|=; 2root(5, 3) + 5sqrt(10) − 6root(5, 3).]

Now, we can combine the two [MATH: \sqrt[3]{5}] terms together:

[MATH: 2root(5, 3) + 5sqrt(10) − 6root(5, 3)|=; 5sqrt(10) + (2root(5, 3) − 6root(5, 3))|=; 5sqrt(10) + (2 − 6)root(5, 3)|=; 5sqrt(10) − 4root(5, 3)]
